title: How to Turn Any Worksheet Into a Classroom Escape Room with NotebookLM
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Alcock gives teachers a step-by-step workflow for wrapping an existing worksheet in a narrative escape room using NotebookLM or Claude. He supplies a single reusable prompt that builds a ten-slide deck with three stages, each tied to problems from the worksheet. He then insists on testing the output against three checks: whether the story is integral rather than decorative, whether the reading level fits the class, and whether each stage differs. His deeper claim is that the escape room's value lies in consequential feedback, where a wrong answer stalls the narrative instead of earning a red mark. The piece sits inside a paid-membership pitch but the workflow itself is concrete and classroom-specific.
points: A single prompt plus an uploaded worksheet can generate a staged escape-room deck without altering any original question.
The narrative must be integrated so students cannot skip the story and still finish the worksheet.
Teachers should check reading level and variety across stages before using AI output.
The pedagogical gain is immediate, consequence-based feedback when errors stop story progress.
Adding a character voice or asking for a plan first are ways to refine the output.
quotes: Not because the maths was wrong. Because there was nothing to enter. No reason to care. No story.
The worksheet stays exactly as it is. The AI doesn’t replace it. It wraps a story around it. Each problem becomes a lock. Each correct answer becomes a key.

This is the step most people skip. They get excited about the output, print it immediately, and hand it to students without checking whether the narrative is doing any actual pedagogical work, or just decorating the page.

Check 1: Can a student skip the story and still complete the worksheet? If yes, the narrative is decoration. It should be integrated, each stage should only reveal the next set of problems after the current ones are solved.
The escape room creates forward pressure. Incorrect answers don’t just get marked wrong, they stall the narrative. That’s a fundamentally different relationship with mistakes.
In conventional worksheet practice, an error is just a red mark at the end. In the escape room version, an error is immediate feedback, the code doesn’t work, the door doesn’t open, the story stops.
